title: Scoliosis treatment for children and young people | NHS inform
text:
Scoliosis treatment for children and young people
Treatment for scoliosis depends on your age, how severe it is, and whether it’s thought it will worsen over time.
Read about scoliosis treatment in adults
Read about scoliosis symptoms, causes and diagnosis
The main treatment options for children and young people are:
observation
casting
bracing
surgery
Observation
Young children don’t always need treatment. Their condition often corrects itself as they grow.
If the curve does not correct itself, it can reduce the space for their internal organs to develop in. This means monitoring by a specialist is important
Your specialist will usually recommend having regular
X-rays
to monitor the curvature. This is to see if it improves, stays the same, or gets worse.
Casting
In some cases affecting young children under 2, the spine may need to be guided during growth using a cast. This is to attempt to correct the curve.
A cast is an external brace. It’s made out of a lightweight combination of plaster and other materials. The cast is worn constantly and cannot be removed.
The cast will be changed under
anaesthetic
every two to three months to allow for growth. The aim is to gradually straighten the spine. Your child may still need to use a removable brace after treatment.
Bracing
If the curve of your or your child’s spine is getting worse, your specialist may recommend wearing a back brace while still growing. A brace cannot cure scoliosis or correct the curve, but it may stop the curve from getting worse.
While there is some evidence bracing may be of benefit in some cases, it’s not recommended by all scoliosis specialists.
If a brace is used, it will need to be carefully fitted to the spine. To do this, a cast of the back may need to be taken. This can be done as an outpatient which means that you or your child will not have to stay overnight in hospital.
Braces are often made of rigid plastic, although flexible braces are sometimes available. Modern back braces are designed so they are difficult to see under loose-fitting clothing.
It’s usually recommended that the brace is worn for 23 hours a day, and is only removed for baths and showers. The brace should not interfere with normal everyday activity. It can be worn during most non-contact sports. It should be removed during contact sports and swimming.
Regular exercise is important for children and young people wearing a brace. This helps improve muscle tone and body strength. It will help make wearing the brace more comfortable.
The brace will usually have to be worn for as long as your or your child’s body is still growing. For most children and young people, this will mean they can stop wearing it when they are around 14 to 16 years old.
Surgery
Surgery on children
Younger children may need an operation to insert growing rods. This is normally carried out in children under 10 years old. The rods allow your child’s spine to continue to grow while partially correcting the scoliosis. Some children may have to wear a brace to protect the rods.
After surgery to insert the rods, your child will need to return to their specialist every 4 to 6 months. This is to have the rods lengthened to keep up with their growth. This procedure is done through a small cut. It takes place often as a day case or an overnight stay.
When your child stops growing, the adjustable rods can be removed and a spinal fusion will be carried out.
Surgery on teenagers and young adults
An operation called a spinal fusion may be carried out on teenagers and young adults whose spine has stopped growing.
This is a major operation where the spine is straightened using metal rods attached with:
screws
hooks
wires
Bone grafts are used to fuse the spine in place. This metalwork will usually be left in place permanently, unless they cause any problems.
The surgery will take several hours. After surgery, you or your child will be transferred to an intensive care unit (ICU) or high dependency unit (HDU). They will be given fluids through a vein (intravenously) and pain relief. Most children are well enough to leave intensive care after a day or two. But, they will often need to spend another 5 to 10 days in hospital.
After the operation, most people can return to school after a few weeks and can play sports after a few months. Contact sports should be avoided for 9-12 months. Occasionally a back brace may need to be worn to protect the metal rods after surgery.
Risks of surgery
Spinal fusion surgery is a major operation. Like any surgical procedure it carries a risk of complications. It will not be recommended unless the surgeon feels the benefits outweigh these risks.
Some of the main risks the spinal fusion procedure include:
bleeding – if this is severe your child may need
a blood transfusion
wound infection – this can usually be treated with
antibiotics
the implants moving or the grafts failing to fuse properly – additional surgery may be needed to correct this.
In rare cases, damage to the nerves in the spine can lead to permanent numbness in the legs
It can also sometimes cause paralysis of the legs and loss of control of the bowels and bladder
It’s important that patients and their families understand the risks of spinal fusion surgery. This will help them make an informed decision about treatment. Make sure you discuss the potential complications with your or your child’s surgeon.
Physiotherapy
Physiotherapy can be beneficial when used along with a back brace. Exercise can help significantly with any muscular pain experienced with scoliosis. It can also help back health in general.
